units.text: 24. How to live without the final explanation

We can now answer the opening question without pretending to close it. Are laws of nature real or imagined? Statements, equations and classifications are human constructions. In many tested situations, the constraints they try to describe do not seem to depend on their formulator’s desire. The existence of additional metaphysical necessity remains disputed. These three answers can be held simultaneously because they answer three different questions.

We need not choose between two caricatures: a universe with a perfect legal code on its walls and a mind arbitrarily inventing every order. There is a world that resists and beings that select, compress and interpret that resistance. Knowing means making selections that remain useful when the world has an opportunity to contradict us.

What did we gain by calling stable relationships ‘laws’? The ability to coordinate experience across generations, build instruments and demand more from an explanation than the speaker’s prestige. What did we risk? Confusing an approximation with destiny, a local regularity with universal necessity and a power relationship with existence’s inevitable order.

This dual power is no reason to abandon the concept. It is a reason to use it with an identification sheet. What does it describe? Under what conditions? With what precision? What observation would challenge it? Who can verify? Who bears the error? The last two questions do not replace physics, but prevent its use as an excuse for unacknowledged allocation of risks.

On emergence, the conclusion is also dual. Stable basic rules can produce new collective relationships and indispensable descriptive levels. It does not follow that every novelty requires breaking physics. But neither does a list of components automatically provide a useful explanation of the whole. Sometimes we must discover suitable variables before recognizing the law.

On mind, it would be wrong to confuse lack of an intuitive image with lack of understanding. We can understand through relationships, consequences and limits, supported by mathematics, instruments and cooperation. It would be equally wrong to confuse a prediction’s success with possession of the final explanation. Mature understanding also knows what it has not obtained.

On simulation, the fruitful question remains conditional. Some implementations might leave traces; others might be observationally indistinct from nonsimulated explanations. Absence of intent to camouflage does not negate the second possibility. Research begins when we choose a precise mechanism class and explain what differences it could produce, not when we declare every anomaly confirms our story.

On morality, neither natural selection, the market nor a cosmic program decides by itself what we owe others. A description of mechanisms helps choose means, anticipate effects and avoid impossible promises. Aims require arguments about values, interests and relationships. Refusing to confuse the two does not weaken science; it asks that science not be used in place of deliberation it cannot replace.

My position is that we need more realism about constraints and less certainty about their ultimate interpretation. Realism prevents us from treating every desire as a solution. Caution prevents us from treating every temporary solution as the universe’s final ruling. Between them lies room for intellectual courage, not merely modesty.

Let us return one last time to the imaginary laboratory. The clocks still disagree. After months of work, perhaps we discover a trivial error. Perhaps we find a physical phenomenon. Perhaps the relationship between observations and explanations changes in a way we cannot yet name. In every variant, the good researcher has gained something: more precise knowledge of what happens and what they are not yet entitled to claim.

The world need not read equations for some equations to describe it well. We must carefully read the conditions under which we use them. And when someone says ‘nature decided’, perhaps the most human question is this: what exactly have we discovered about the world, and what exactly are we trying to stop discussing among ourselves?
